entries.title: Context multiplier
entries.tip: Your 10th message can cost 11x more than your first because Claude rereads the full conversation each turn.

entries.title: Output also counts
entries.tip: Every word Claude generates is billed too. Shorter answers save both input and output tokens.

entries.title: Edit, don't follow up
entries.tip: Instead of sending a correction message when Claude makes a mistake, click 'edit' on your original prompt and fix the wording. This replaces the exchange in the history rather than adding to it.

entries.title: Batch your questions
entries.tip: Combine multiple tasks into a single message. One prompt with three tasks equals one context load, whereas three separate messages result in three context loads.

entries.title: Fresh chat every 15–20
entries.tip: Start a new conversation every 15 to 20 messages. Ask Claude to summarize the current chat first, then paste that summary as the starting point of the new chat to ditch the bloat.

entries.title: Use fewer tokens
entries.tip: Shift your mindset from counting messages to counting tokens. Since Claude rereads the entire history every turn, the 10th message costs significantly more than the first.

entries.title: Track token usage
entries.tip: Install a local dashboard or check your machine's JSONL log files to see real input/output token data. You can't fix what you can't measure.

entries.title: Upload to projects
entries.tip: Upload recurring files (PDFs, style guides, contracts) to the 'Projects' feature once. This allows Claude to reference them without retokenizing the document every time.

entries.title: Set up memory
entries.tip: Use 'Memory and User Settings' to save your role and communication style permanently. This stops you from burning tokens on 'Act as a...' setup prompts in every chat.

entries.title: Turn off unused features
entries.tip: Disable web search, connectors, and 'Advanced Thinking' if you don't need them. These features add tokens to every response.

entries.title: Use Haiku for simple tasks
entries.tip: Use the Haiku model for brainstorming, formatting, or grammar checks. It handles these tasks at a much lower cost than Sonnet or Opus.

entries.title: Enable overage safety net
entries.tip: Enable the overage feature in usage settings. This switches to pay-as-you-go billing at API rates when limits are hit, so you don't lose work.

entries.title: Spread work sessions
entries.tip: Claude uses a rolling 5-hour window. Divide your work into morning, afternoon, and evening sessions to let your usage reset throughout the day.

entries.title: Work during off-peak
entries.tip: Perform resource-intensive tasks in the evening or on weekends. Usage limits may be consumed more quickly during peak hours (5 AM–11 AM PT).

entries.title: Early morning ping
entries.tip: Send a tiny message early in the morning (e.g., 6 AM) to start your rolling 5-hour window before you actually sit down to work.

entries.title: Talk like a caveman
entries.tip: Instruct Claude to drop the fluff and talk like a caveman. This can reduce output token consumption by up to 65%.

entries.title: Cache stable prefixes
entries.tip: For API workflows, put stable system instructions, tools, examples, and background context before the changing user request so prompt caching can reuse the shared prefix.

entries.title: Keep changing data last
entries.tip: Place volatile inputs — the latest bug report, pasted diff, or question — after the reusable context. Stable-first ordering makes cached prompts more effective.

entries.title: Summarize huge tool output
entries.tip: When a command produces pages of logs, ask Claude to keep only the failing command, error block, environment, and next action. Raw repeated logs quickly bloat the chat.

entries.title: Trim old screenshots
entries.tip: For UI work, replace old screenshots with a short visual summary once the issue is understood. Images can be expensive context if they stay in every turn.

entries.title: Use explicit stop points
entries.tip: For long work, tell Claude exactly when to pause, summarize, or compact. This preserves the important state before the conversation gets heavy.

entries.title: Use Haiku for sub-agents
entries.tip: Run simpler sub-agent tasks on the Haiku model while keeping the main session on a stronger model for final decisions.

entries.title: Anchor on concrete outputs
entries.tip: Tell Claude exactly what file, function, or artifact it should produce — vague goals cause wandering.

entries.title: Break long pipelines
entries.tip: Split multi-step agent tasks into discrete checkpoints. Verify each step before moving to the next.

entries.title: Define abort conditions
entries.tip: Tell Claude when to stop and report back rather than keep trying — e.g. 'if you can't find it in 3 attempts, halt'.

entries.title: Dry-run first
entries.tip: Ask Claude to describe the actions it intends to take before it takes them. Catch mistakes before they run.

entries.title: Gate destructive actions
entries.tip: Instruct Claude to ask before deleting files, sending messages, or making API writes.

entries.title: Parallelize sub-tasks
entries.tip: For independent sub-tasks (e.g. research + code + docs), launch them as separate chats and merge results.

entries.title: State your success criteria
entries.tip: Include a measurable outcome in your prompt — 'done when all tests pass' beats 'make it work'.

entries.title: Use structured output
entries.tip: Ask for JSON or XML when the result feeds another process. Structured output is easier to parse and validate.

entries.title: Give tool permissions by class
entries.tip: State which actions are safe automatically, which require confirmation, and which are forbidden. Agents behave better when permission boundaries are explicit.

entries.title: Require a discovery pass
entries.tip: Before edits, ask Claude to inspect the repository, identify relevant files, and report the likely change surface. This prevents drive-by patches in the wrong module.

entries.title: Ask for checkpoints
entries.tip: For multi-file changes, have Claude stop after each meaningful checkpoint with what changed, what passed, and what remains.

entries.title: Separate read and write phases
entries.tip: Tell Claude to read, analyze, and plan first, then edit only after the plan is coherent. This reduces accidental rewrites.

entries.title: Make rollback easy
entries.tip: Ask Claude to group changes so they can be reverted cleanly. Small reversible steps are safer than one giant agentic sweep.

entries.title: Keep stateful stages rare
entries.tip: Use a persistent SDK session only where prior turns matter. Run independent stages as fresh queries to avoid conversational residue.

entries.title: Control the event stream
entries.tip: Treat session events as the control plane. Watch idle states, stop reasons, and required actions instead of relying only on final text.

entries.title: Deploy sub-agents for parallel work
entries.tip: Launch isolated sub-agents for independent research, tests, or drafts, then merge their findings into the main session.

entries.title: Build custom skills
entries.tip: Create reusable skills or prompt files for common workflows so the same strategy works consistently across sessions.

entries.title: Use agent teams
entries.tip: Use agents that can talk to each other and share a task list for more coherent parallel collaboration.

entries.title: Keep claude.md lean
entries.tip: Keep your claude.md project file lean (under 200 lines) and use it as an index.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Limit unused MCP servers
entries.tip: Limit MCP servers and Claude skills to only those used in at least 20% of sessions.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Manually compact chat
entries.tip: Manually compact the chat when usage reaches 50–60%.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Monitor token usage
entries.tip: Use '/context' and 'status line' commands in Claude Code to monitor token usage.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Respect the cache rule
entries.tip: Mind the 'Five-Minute Cache Rule' — reprocess after inactivity to avoid spikes.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Save preferences
entries.tip: Save your role, style, and formatting once in memory instead of retyping it every new chat.

entries.title: Save progress before compacting
entries.tip: Save progress and update progress/plan files before compacting or taking a break.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Upload recurring files
entries.tip: Put repeated documents in Projects once. Cached content avoids repeated retokenization.

entries.title: Preserve decisions in compaction
entries.tip: When compacting, specifically preserve architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, chosen constraints, and file paths. These are the details most painful to rediscover.

entries.title: Discard raw tool noise
entries.tip: After a tool result has served its purpose, summarize the useful conclusion and remove or ignore the raw output. The conclusion matters more than the scrollback.

entries.title: Keep a living project brief
entries.tip: Maintain a short project brief with goals, constraints, commands, and current status. Point Claude to that instead of re-explaining the project every session.

entries.title: Pin current files
entries.tip: Name the few files currently in play and why they matter. Claude performs better when the active working set is obvious.

entries.title: Compress before task switching
entries.tip: Before jumping from implementation to docs or design, ask for a state summary. Topic switches are where context loss gets sneaky.

entries.title: Separate memory policy
entries.tip: Put what belongs in memory in the store description. Put how to use it this session in the session instructions.

entries.title: Thread equals session
entries.tip: For chat bots, map each thread ID to one session ID. Replies in the same thread keep conversation and filesystem context together.

entries.title: Attach memory early
entries.tip: Memory stores must be attached when the session starts. Files can be added later, so design memory as early-bound context.

entries.title: Keep context small
entries.tip: Only give Claude the files and details needed for the current task. Smaller context windows reduce noise and improve response quality.

entries.title: Use /context to diagnose bloat
entries.tip: Run /context to see what is eating your token budget and rethink the prompt if system or file content is dominating.

entries.title: Compact and clear regularly
entries.tip: Use /compact and /clear when your session feels bloated. Preserve important decisions, then reset the noisy history.

entries.title: Refresh cloud.md often
entries.tip: Update your cloud.md whenever you discover new project conventions, patterns, or gotchas so the next session starts smarter.

entries.title: Route context from cloud.md
entries.tip: Keep cloud.md lean and point it to external style guides, docs, and reference files instead of putting everything in one place.

entries.title: Always include a test case
entries.tip: Provide sample input and expected output in your prompt. Claude writes tighter code when it can self-check.

entries.title: Ask for comments sparingly
entries.tip: Request inline comments only for non-obvious logic. Excessive comments inflate output tokens with little value.

entries.title: Constrain the interface
entries.tip: Specify the exact function signature, class structure, or API contract before asking Claude to implement it.

entries.title: Diff before accepting
entries.tip: For edits to existing code, ask Claude to show a diff view. Review changes before pasting in.

entries.title: Name the language explicitly
entries.tip: Say 'Python 3.11' not just 'Python' — version hints prevent deprecated patterns.

entries.title: Pass failing tests as context
entries.tip: Paste the test that's failing alongside the code. Claude fixes the right thing when it sees both.

entries.title: Pin your dependencies
entries.tip: Include the library name and version when asking for integration code. Avoids outdated API calls.

entries.title: Request minimal diffs
entries.tip: Ask Claude to change only what's necessary. 'Keep the rest of the file intact' prevents over-editing.

entries.title: Show the error message
entries.tip: Copy the exact error text into your prompt. Stack traces and error codes beat vague descriptions.

entries.title: Specify the output format
entries.tip: For scripts, say 'print to stdout', 'return a dict', or 'write to file'. Ambiguity wastes iterations.

entries.title: Use Plan Mode
entries.tip: Use Plan Mode to avoid wasted tokens on incorrect directions.
entries.source: Stop Wasting Your Claude Tokens. Do This Instead... by Rick Mulready

entries.title: Ask for codebase conventions
entries.tip: Before generating code, ask Claude to infer naming, error handling, formatting, and file organization from nearby files.

entries.title: Prefer narrow file edits
entries.tip: Tell Claude the exact file or function to modify when possible. Narrow targets reduce hallucinated helpers and unnecessary rewrites.

entries.title: Request command-ready output
entries.tip: Ask Claude to include the exact test, build, or lint commands it expects you to run after the change.

entries.title: Give acceptance examples
entries.tip: For UI or API behavior, provide one accepted example and one rejected example. Claude can match concrete behavior better than vibes.

entries.title: Mark generated sections
entries.tip: When Claude creates boilerplate, ask it to mark generated sections clearly. Future edits become easier and safer.

entries.title: Make reporting tool-free
entries.tip: After triage, stop using tools and generate strict structured output. Required fields and nulls make downstream parsing safer.

entries.title: Fragment Plotly charts
entries.tip: For multi-chart HTML reports, export Plotly fragments and load Plotly once in the head. Avoid duplicate JavaScript per chart.

entries.title: Bisect the problem
entries.tip: Ask Claude to identify which half of the code contains the bug before attempting a fix.

entries.title: Check assumptions first
entries.tip: Before diving into a fix, ask Claude to list its assumptions. Wrong assumptions cause wrong fixes.

entries.title: Give full stack traces
entries.tip: Paste the complete traceback, not just the last line. Context lines often contain the real cause.

entries.title: Isolate the repro case
entries.tip: Ask Claude to produce the smallest code snippet that reproduces the issue before adding a fix.

entries.title: Name the environment
entries.tip: OS, runtime version, and framework matter. 'Python 3.11 on macOS ARM' beats 'my machine'.

entries.title: Provide before/after
entries.tip: Show what used to work and what changed. Regression bugs are much faster to fix with a changelog.

entries.title: Request root cause first
entries.tip: Ask 'What is causing this?' before 'Fix it'. Understanding the cause often reveals a better solution.

entries.title: Ask for a failure tree
entries.tip: Have Claude list the top likely causes ranked by probability before changing code. Debugging becomes a search problem, not a guessing game.

entries.title: Keep one variable moving
entries.tip: Ask Claude to change only one thing per experiment. Multiple simultaneous fixes make it impossible to know what worked.

entries.title: Capture the exact command
entries.tip: Paste the command that produced the error, not just the error. Flags, working directory, and shell matter.

entries.title: Compare expected paths
entries.tip: When files are missing or imports fail, ask Claude to trace expected path vs. actual path before editing.

entries.title: Log before rewriting
entries.tip: Ask Claude to add temporary targeted logs before proposing a large refactor. Observation beats heroic surgery.

entries.title: Ask for trade-offs
entries.tip: Request pros/cons or multiple approaches before committing. Prevents lock-in to a suboptimal path.

entries.title: Define constraints up front
entries.tip: State performance targets, size limits, and compatibility requirements before asking for a design.

entries.title: Generate an ADR
entries.tip: Ask Claude to produce an Architecture Decision Record for major choices. Great for team knowledge transfer.

entries.title: Map dependencies first
entries.tip: Before writing code, ask Claude to map all dependencies and interactions. Catches integration issues early.

entries.title: Plan in plain language
entries.tip: Get a written plan approved before any code is generated. Cheap to change text, expensive to change code.

entries.title: Request a checklist
entries.tip: For complex tasks, ask Claude to generate a checklist first. Use it to track completion without re-explaining context.

entries.title: Separate design from implementation
entries.tip: Ask for schema or interface design in one message, implementation in the next. Each step stays focused.

entries.title: Work top-down
entries.tip: Start with system design, then modules, then functions. Claude produces more coherent code with the big picture.

entries.title: Ask for non-goals
entries.tip: Have Claude list what the system will not do. Non-goals prevent scope creep and make architecture sharper.

entries.title: Define ownership boundaries
entries.tip: Ask Claude to specify which module owns each responsibility. Blurry ownership causes tangled code later.

entries.title: Document invariants
entries.tip: Ask for the rules that must always remain true, such as data ordering, identity stability, or threading constraints.

entries.title: Request migration steps
entries.tip: For refactors, ask Claude to design a safe migration path from the current system to the desired system.

entries.title: Include failure modes
entries.tip: Ask Claude how the design fails under load, bad data, network loss, or partial writes before implementation begins.

entries.title: Layer tools by trust
entries.tip: Use sandbox tools for local work, Skills for team conventions, and custom tools only for external side effects.

entries.title: Keep agents reusable
entries.tip: Put the repeatable workflow in the agent. Send the current alert, dataset, or request as session data instead.

entries.title: Separate durable resources
entries.tip: Treat agents, environments, and memory stores as reusable definitions. Treat sessions as disposable per-task runtimes.

entries.title: Make paths contracts
entries.tip: Use stable paths for memory, inputs, and outputs. Filesystem layout becomes the contract between agent and app.

entries.title: Always start in plan mode
entries.tip: Use plan mode first to outline steps, ask questions, and map the approach before writing code.

entries.title: Use UltraThink for hard decisions
entries.tip: When the task is complex or uncertain, invoke UltraThink so Claude uses a larger reasoning budget before responding.

entries.title: Add a persona
entries.tip: Assigning a role ('you are a senior security engineer') focuses Claude's vocabulary and priorities.

entries.title: Assign explicit constraints
entries.tip: Hard constraints beat soft ones. 'Do not use external libraries' is clearer than 'try to minimize dependencies'.

entries.title: Chain-of-thought for hard problems
entries.tip: Add 'think step by step' for math, logic, or planning tasks. Dramatically reduces errors on multi-step reasoning.

entries.title: Few-shot examples work
entries.tip: Provide 2–3 input/output examples in your prompt for format-sensitive tasks. Better than describing the format in words.

entries.title: Give negative examples too
entries.tip: Show Claude what you don't want alongside what you do. Reduces the chance of drifting toward common but wrong patterns.

entries.title: Ground with real data
entries.tip: Paste in real filenames, real error messages, real schema names. Specificity dramatically improves quality.

entries.title: Separate context from instruction
entries.tip: Use clear delimiters (e.g. <doc>...</doc>) to separate background context from the actual task.

entries.title: Specify the audience
entries.tip: 'Explain to a junior developer' vs. 'explain to a principal engineer' yields very different, more useful answers.

entries.title: Temperature via words
entries.tip: Say 'be creative and explore unusual options' or 'be conservative and follow best practices' instead of adjusting sliders.

entries.title: Use XML for structure
entries.tip: Wrapping context in XML tags (<instructions>, <context>, <examples>) produces more reliable parsing by Claude.

entries.title: Use task brackets
entries.tip: Wrap instructions, context, examples, and output format in separate tags so Claude does not confuse background material with the actual request.

entries.title: Tell Claude what to ignore
entries.tip: If pasted context includes outdated plans or irrelevant logs, explicitly mark them as reference-only or deprecated.

entries.title: Put the ask last
entries.tip: For long prompts, end with a short, explicit task statement. Claude is less likely to miss the real job.

entries.title: Request uncertainty labels
entries.tip: Ask Claude to mark guesses, assumptions, and verified facts separately when accuracy matters.

entries.title: Use reusable prompt shells
entries.tip: Create templates with slots for context, constraints, examples, and output format. Consistent structure gives more consistent answers.

entries.title: Prompt the workflow only
entries.tip: Keep the system prompt generic. Send incident-specific or user-specific details as the first user event.

entries.title: Treat Claude like a junior developer
entries.tip: Ask Claude to solve problems instead of only giving direct commands. Let it think through the approach and then review the assumptions.

entries.title: Make Claude ask questions
entries.tip: Tell Claude to ask clarifying questions until it is highly confident it understands the task. Alignment improves faster than guesswork.

entries.title: Exit early and reask
entries.tip: If Claude starts down the wrong path, stop it and correct course immediately. Early redirection saves tokens and prevents wasted work.

entries.title: Challenge outputs aggressively
entries.tip: If the first result is just okay, ask for a more elegant or completely different approach. Higher standards lead to better revisions.

entries.title: Ask for citations
entries.tip: For research tasks, ask Claude to include citations or note when it's uncertain. Reduces hallucination risk.

entries.title: Draft then refine
entries.tip: Get a rough draft first, then ask for targeted rewrites. Cheaper than generating polished prose in one shot.

entries.title: Give a word count
entries.tip: Specify 'about 200 words' or 'at least 400 words'. Vague length requests produce wildly inconsistent output.

entries.title: Request an outline first
entries.tip: For long documents, get an outline approved before generating full content. Prevents wasted prose.

entries.title: Set the reading level
entries.tip: 'Write at a 5th grade reading level' or 'assume PhD-level reader' tunes vocabulary and sentence complexity.

entries.title: Specify tone explicitly
entries.tip: 'Formal', 'conversational', 'technical', 'enthusiastic' — tone words do more work than vague quality adjectives.

entries.title: Summarize long docs first
entries.tip: Paste a long document and ask for a summary before asking specific questions. Orients Claude to the material.

entries.title: Ask for source tiers
entries.tip: Tell Claude which sources count as primary, secondary, or unacceptable. This keeps research from leaning on weak summaries.

entries.title: Separate facts from synthesis
entries.tip: Ask Claude to list sourced facts first, then analysis. This makes it easier to spot unsupported leaps.

entries.title: Request quote limits
entries.tip: For copyrighted or sensitive sources, ask for brief quotes plus paraphrase. You get evidence without turning the answer into a copied article.

entries.title: Give a publication target
entries.tip: Say whether the output is for an email, blog post, investor memo, support reply, or technical doc. Claude will choose a better structure.

entries.title: Ask for revision notes
entries.tip: After a rewrite, ask Claude to summarize what changed and why. This makes editing feel intentional instead of mysterious.

entries.title: Clone inspiration sites
entries.tip: Feed screenshots or examples of a design you like and ask Claude to apply that visual language, not just generic AI styling.

entries.title: Audit Claude's code
entries.tip: Treat Claude-generated code as a junior dev's PR — review for security issues before merging to production.

entries.title: Never paste credentials
entries.tip: Scrub API keys, tokens, and passwords from any code before pasting into a chat prompt.

entries.title: Redact PII
entries.tip: Replace real names, emails, and personal data with placeholders before sharing logs or data files.

entries.title: Sanitize before paste
entries.tip: Strip internal URLs, hostnames, and internal identifiers from prompts shared in logged sessions.

entries.title: Test in sandbox first
entries.tip: Run Claude-generated scripts in a sandbox or staging environment before touching production.

entries.title: Validate external sources
entries.tip: If Claude fetches or references external data, verify URLs and sources before trusting the output.

entries.title: Use least privilege prompts
entries.tip: For agentic coding, grant only the minimum commands and folders needed for the task. Broad permission invites accidental damage.

entries.title: Block secret exfiltration
entries.tip: Tell Claude never to print, summarize, or transmit secret-looking values from env files, logs, or config.

entries.title: Review dependency changes
entries.tip: Ask Claude to justify new dependencies and flag license, maintenance, and supply-chain concerns before adding them.

entries.title: Prefer dry-run commands
entries.tip: Use dry-run, preview, or no-write flags before allowing scripts to modify files or infrastructure.

entries.title: Use disposable worktrees
entries.tip: Run risky Claude Code experiments in a fresh branch, worktree, container, or sandbox so mistakes are isolated.

entries.title: Do not trust allowed_tools
entries.tip: In the Agent SDK, allowed_tools auto-approves tools; it is not a hard whitelist. Use disallowed_tools for real denial.

entries.title: Keep reference memory read-only
entries.tip: Use read-write memory for user preferences only. Attach shared reference material as read-only to avoid memory poisoning.

entries.title: Approve only the merge
entries.tip: Let agents investigate and prepare changes freely. Put the human checkpoint at the irreversible merge or deploy boundary.

entries.title: Limit container networking
entries.tip: Disabling web_search is not sandbox isolation. Use limited networking and explicit allowed hosts for production agents.

entries.title: Deny explicitly
entries.tip: When a tool must never run, deny it explicitly. Do not assume omission from auto-approved tools blocks access.

entries.title: Edit permissions for safe autonomy
entries.tip: Explicitly allow only safe commands and deny destructive ones. You get faster agent autonomy without giving up safety.

entries.title: Ask Claude to break its own code
entries.tip: After generating a function, ask Claude to list edge cases and failure modes it didn't handle.

entries.title: Generate test cases separately
entries.tip: Ask for tests in a separate prompt from the implementation. Mixed prompts produce incomplete coverage.

entries.title: Mutation testing prompts
entries.tip: Ask Claude to deliberately introduce bugs, then fix them. Confirms your tests actually catch issues.

entries.title: Request property-based tests
entries.tip: For data-heavy logic, ask for property-based tests (e.g. Hypothesis/fast-check). Finds edge cases automatically.

entries.title: Review assertions explicitly
entries.tip: Ask Claude to explain why each assertion is correct. Surfaces wrong tests that pass for the wrong reason.

entries.title: Test error paths
entries.tip: Ask specifically for tests that cover failure modes — not just the happy path.

entries.title: Ask for test intent
entries.tip: Have Claude explain what each test proves before writing the test body. Intent-first tests are less brittle.

entries.title: Run smallest tests first
entries.tip: Ask Claude to identify the fastest targeted test command before running the full suite.

entries.title: Add regression tests
entries.tip: When fixing a bug, require a test that fails before the fix and passes after it.

entries.title: Check generated tests for tautologies
entries.tip: Ask Claude to make sure tests do not simply duplicate the implementation logic. Tests should verify behavior, not mirror code.

entries.title: Ask for quality gates
entries.tip: Define the exact checks required before calling work done: tests, lint, typecheck, build, docs, or manual QA.

entries.title: Use a triage pass
entries.tip: Find issues first, then re-judge them in a fresh pass. Re-check source lines, merge duplicates, and recompute severity.

entries.title: Analyze with code first
entries.tip: For data work, make Claude write scripts, sample tables, and sanity-check metrics before writing the narrative.

entries.title: Rubric before review
entries.tip: Give the finder a quality rubric before it searches. It should know which findings are real and which are noise.

entries.title: Build self-checking todo lists
entries.tip: Have Claude add verification steps after each task, such as screenshots or browser checks, before moving on.

entries.title: Use screenshots for UI validation
entries.tip: Capture page screenshots and ask Claude whether the layout, spacing, and content look correct.

entries.title: Use Chrome DevTools for functional checks
entries.tip: Have Claude interact with the browser and examine the live app to validate buttons, forms, and app behavior.

entries.title: Chain outputs as inputs
entries.tip: Pass Claude's JSON output directly into the next prompt as structured input. Reduces re-typing and parsing errors.

entries.title: Create reusable templates
entries.tip: For recurring tasks (PR descriptions, changelogs, release notes), build fill-in-the-blank prompt templates.

entries.title: Integrate with your editor
entries.tip: Use Claude Code CLI or a VS Code extension so you can invoke Claude without switching windows.

entries.title: Pipe CLI output directly
entries.tip: Redirect terminal output (logs, test results) directly into a Claude prompt with heredoc or piping.

entries.title: Use Projects for team context
entries.tip: Store shared system prompts, style guides, and codebase docs in a Project so the whole team stays aligned.

entries.title: Wire into CI
entries.tip: Use Claude API in CI to auto-generate PR summaries, flag risky diffs, or suggest test names for new functions.

entries.title: Connect Claude to the repo
entries.tip: Use Claude Code in the terminal or IDE when the task requires reading and editing multiple files. Copy-paste chat is better for small, isolated questions.

entries.title: Automate release notes
entries.tip: Feed merged commits or PR summaries into Claude and ask for customer-facing release notes plus developer changelog bullets.

entries.title: Create handoff packets
entries.tip: At the end of a session, ask Claude for a handoff containing status, changed files, commands run, open risks, and next steps.

entries.title: Use issue-shaped prompts
entries.tip: Write prompts like tickets: problem, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, and verification plan.

entries.title: Keep integrations visible
entries.tip: List which tools Claude may use — editor, terminal, GitHub, CI, browser, docs — so it chooses the right workflow instead of guessing.

entries.title: Memory is product state
entries.tip: Persist a user-to-store mapping in your app. Seed memory from product data and expose a review surface for corrections.

entries.title: Webhook required actions
entries.tip: Use a session.requires_action webhook in production. Polling notebooks are fine for demos, not deployed approvals.

entries.title: Preload the environment
entries.tip: Install common packages in the environment definition. Cached dependencies make sessions faster and more reproducible.

entries.title: Write outputs deliberately
entries.tip: Put final deliverables in /mnt/session/outputs/. Treat every other path as scratch unless your app owns it.

entries.title: Reuse bot resources
entries.tip: Persist environment ID, agent ID, and agent version. Reuse them for every mention instead of rebuilding per request.

entries.title: Ack chat events first
entries.tip: Acknowledge chat platform events immediately. Do file uploads, session creation, and stream relay in background work.

entries.title: Post only downloads
entries.tip: When listing session files, filter for downloadable outputs before reposting results back into chat.

entries.title: Run /init on every project
entries.tip: Start by opening the repo and running /init so Claude scans the codebase and builds a project cheat sheet.

entries.title: Set up a status line
entries.tip: Use a status line to surface model, context usage, and cost in real time while you work.

entries.title: Use voice input when available
entries.tip: Use /voice or a dictation tool to speak prompts directly, speeding up your workflow for planning and quick notes.

entries.title: Use /re for quick undos
entries.tip: Rollback to a previous point with /re when a direction is wrong instead of letting the session keep drifting.

entries.title: Use hooks for session notifications
entries.tip: Configure notification hooks so you get alerted when a session completes or requires your attention.

entries.title: Run parallel sessions with worktrees
entries.tip: Use Git worktrees or branches for isolated Claude sessions so experiments don't overwrite each other's files.

entries.title: Use API endpoints instead of MCP servers
entries.tip: For narrow tasks, call the direct API endpoint instead of loading full MCP tool definitions into the context.

entries.title: Use /loop for recurring checks
